findings.title: Denial cache reintroduces the 'cannot access newly created resource' bug the PR fixes
findings.body: The permDenialCache entry for (namespace, user, action, name, parentFolder) is set with a 30s TTL whenever a Check is denied, and any later Check with the same key short-circuits to denied before the permission cache or DB is consulted (service.go:116-121). Consider the exact scenario the PR describes: a user without a scoped permission triggers a Check for e.g. dashboards:read on name 'newdash' in folder 'fold1' (e.g. a pre-flight check, a duplicate-name check, or a failed attempt), which populates a denial entry. The user then creates the dashboard/folder, which writes the permission row to the DB. The next Check for that same (user, action, name, folder) hits the denial cache and returns Allowed=false without ever re-querying the DB — so the creator is still locked out of their newly created resource for up to 30 seconds. Any mechanism that invalidates/refreshes permCache (e.g. a DB requery triggered by a different resource name) does not invalidate the denial entry, so the denial can even outlive a freshly queried permission map that would allow the request. The denial cache needs to be invalidated when permissions change (e.g. on permission/role writes or resource creation), or its scope/TTL must be bounded so it cannot mask fresh grants.

findings.title: Denial cache key uses the raw subject identifier, not the resolved user UID
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey is built from checkReq.UserUID (the raw ID parsed from the subject string), whereas the permission cache key (userPermCacheKey) is built from the resolved userIdentifiers.UID obtained via GetUserIdentifiers (service.go:360, 379). Since GetUserIdentifiers accepts both numeric user IDs and UIDs as the subject identifier (service.go:463-469), the same user can be addressed as 'user:112' or 'user:<uid>'. The denial decision was computed from the resolved identity's permissions, but it is stored under the caller-supplied identifier. Consequences: (1) denial entries are not shared between the two spellings, causing unnecessary duplicate DB requeries; (2) if the mapping between a numeric ID and UID ever changes (user deletion/recreation), a stale denial entry keyed by the numeric ID remains valid and keeps denying the new identity for up to 30s. The key should use the resolved UID, consistent with the permission cache.

findings.title: Denial-cache hits are counted as permission-cache hits in metrics
findings.body: When the denial cache short-circuits a Check, the code increments s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage with label "true" (cache hit). This conflates the new denial cache with the permission cache, making the permissionCacheUsage metric misleading for operators tuning cache behavior: a denial hit is reported as a permission cache hit even though the permission cache was never consulted. A separate label or metric (e.g. permissionDenialCacheUsage) should be used.

findings.title: No test covers the denial cache being populated by a denied Check and its interaction with later allowed checks
findings.body: The only denial-cache test ('Should deny on explicit cache deny entry') manually pre-populates permDenialCache; there is no test that a Check returning Allowed=false actually writes a denial entry and that a subsequent identical Check short-circuits without touching the store. More importantly, there is no test for the interaction the feature exists for: after a denial is cached, a subsequent grant of the permission in the store (simulating resource creation) — the 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' sibling case where permCache/DB allow but the denial entry denies. Without such a test the stale-denial regression risk (denial entry masking a fresh DB allow) is unguarded.
